title: Strong universal online learning with arbitrary responses
formal: For every nonempty separable metrizable input space \(X\) and every nonempty separable metric output space \((Y,\ell)\) of diameter at most one, is there a single online learning rule \(F\) with the following property? For every joint stochastic process \((X_t,Y_t)_{t\ge1}\) whose input marginal belongs to \(\mathrm{SUOL}(X,Y,\ell)\), and for every Borel measurable comparator \(g:X\to Y\), \[\limsup_{T\to\infty}\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^{T}\bigl(\ell(\widehat Y_t,Y_t)-\ell(g(X_t),Y_t)\bigr)\le0\quad\text{almost surely},\] where \(\widehat Y_t=F_t(X_1,Y_1,\ldots,X_{t-1},Y_{t-1},X_t,U)\)? The rule may depend on the two spaces and their loss, but not on the process or comparator. The responses may have arbitrary dependence on the entire input process and on one another; they need not be values of any fixed target function.
why: The question tests whether arbitrary response noise imposes an additional obstacle beyond the input-process conditions needed for noiseless universal learning. Its resolution shows that the geometry of the output loss can change the answer, even when that loss is bounded, clarifying the reach of universal online prediction.
status_note: Resolved negatively in the stated generality by Blanchard and Jaillet, Annals of Statistics 2023. On 2026-09-14, checked the author manuscript v3, Section 3’s explicit restatement and Theorem 5.1, and verified journal publication metadata via Crossref. The positive totally bounded cases are preserved in context. This review checks theorem scope rather than independently formalizing its proof.

progress.text: Hanneke states Open Problem 1 after proving arbitrary-response consistency under a stronger condition on input processes.

Blanchard and Jaillet publish a characterization of arbitrary-response universal learning. The checked June 2023 manuscript explicitly identifies Hanneke’s question; Theorem 5.1 provides the general counterexample, while Corollary 4.4 supplies the totally bounded positive case.

importance.reason: A broad question about the difference between noiseless and arbitrary-response universal online learning; the resolved dependence on the output metric identifies a structural limit beyond stationarity and binary classification.

sentences: The question asks for one online learner covering every input process that allows noiseless universal learning.
The same learner must compete with every fixed measurable predictor when responses are arbitrarily dependent.
The source allows every bounded separable metric output space.
Blanchard and Jaillet give a counterexample in that generality, while proving positive results for totally bounded output spaces.
The resolved distinction shows that the output loss geometry affects whether arbitrary responses impose an additional learning barrier.

definitions:
A separable metric space has a countable dense subset; its Borel sigma-algebra is generated by its open sets. Equip all finite and infinite products here with their product sigma-algebras. A metric \(\ell\) is nonnegative and symmetric, vanishes exactly on equal points, and satisfies the triangle inequality; the diameter assumption means \(\ell(y,y')\le1\) for all outputs. An input space is separable metrizable if some metric inducing its topology has a countable dense subset. Each process is an arbitrary probability law on the sequence of Borel input–output pairs. There is no independence, stationarity or ergodicity assumption on the data.

An online rule is a sequence of measurable maps \(F_t:(X\times Y)^{t-1}\times X\times[0,1]\to Y\). A seed \(U\) is uniform on \([0,1]\) and independent of the entire data process. At time \(t\), the learner sees \(X_t\) and past pairs, predicts, and then observes \(Y_t\). Computability, time bounds and a finite-sample rate are not required. A deterministic rule can ignore its seed. Almost-sure guarantees are over both the data and seed, separately for each fixed process and comparator; one common probability-one event for every measurable comparator is not required.

An input-process law \(P_X\) is in \(\mathrm{SUOL}(X,Y,\ell)\) if there exists an online rule \(G\), possibly depending on \(P_X\), such that for every Borel measurable \(g:X\to Y\), when \(Y_t=g(X_t)\), the average loss \(T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ell(\widehat Y_t,g(X_t))\) tends to zero almost surely. Thus membership says that one rule works for every noiseless target on that fixed input process. The question instead demands one rule for all such input laws with arbitrary responses, and compares its average loss with each fixed measurable predictor.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of this universal existence claim, or of its negation. A negative answer may give input and output spaces for which no rule has the stated guarantee: every candidate must fail for some admissible joint process and comparator with positive probability. A result restricted to binary outputs or to totally bounded output spaces does not prove the universal claim. Its negative resolution for general bounded separable metric outputs is published; an existing Lean formalization is not asserted.

context_blocks.text: The comparator is a fixed measurable function of the current input. Responses need not equal that function, so zero average prediction loss would be an inappropriate general target. The requirement concerns the excess loss relative to the comparator.

The source had already established arbitrary-response consistency for a substantial family of input processes including stationary ones. Its Open Problem 1 asks whether the entire noiselessly learnable family can be covered. This card retains the full bounded separable metric setting, rather than silently restricting the output space to binary labels.

Blanchard and Jaillet give a negative answer in that generality. Their Theorem 5.1 constructs a countable output space with a bounded metric, with distances zero, one half and one, for which some noiselessly learnable input processes do not permit arbitrary-response universal learning.

They also prove positive results for totally bounded output spaces, including finite classification and bounded intervals with their usual metric. A metric space is totally bounded if for every positive radius it has a finite cover by balls of that radius. Thus the negative answer for general bounded metric spaces does not negate these important positive cases.
